title: Drawdown, Exposure, Sensitivity and Hedging
objectives: Compute running peaks, drawdowns and maximum drawdown on a value series
Explain why drawdown matters to investors beyond volatility
Quantify exposure and sensitivity (beta, duration, DV01) for a position
Size a hedge from a sensitivity and check what risk remains after hedging
motivation: Volatility treats a +10% day and a -10% day symmetrically; investors do not. Drawdown measures the actual peak-to-trough pain an investor must sit through, and behavioural finance (plus redemption clauses) makes that pain economically real. This lesson computes drawdowns from a series and then covers the other half of risk management practice: measuring exposure through sensitivities and laying hedges against them.

blocks.caption: Drawdown at time $t$: distance below the running peak

blocks.md: The **maximum drawdown** (MaxDD) is the most negative value this ever reaches. Work through a hypothetical fund's weekly values in \$k: $100,\ 110,\ 105,\ 118,\ 112,\ 96,\ 104,\ 121,\ 116,\ 130$.

blocks.title: Computing drawdowns step by step
items: Running peak: $100 \to 110 \to 110 \to 118 \to 118 \to 118 \to 118 \to 121 \to 121 \to 130$ (a peak only updates when the value exceeds everything before it).
**MaxDD = -18.6%**: from the 118 peak to the 96 trough, a \$22k fall on a \$118k peak.
Recovery: the fund only re-topped at 121 (week 8), it spent four weeks 'underwater' after the trough.
Note the asymmetry: a $-18.6\%$ drawdown needs a $+22/96 = +22.9\%$ gain to recover. Losses and gains are not symmetric in percentage space.

blocks.md: Why investors care more about MaxDD than volatility: drawdown is path-dependent, two funds with identical volatility can have very different worst-peak-to-trough paths, and redemption decisions, margin calls and career risk all key off the drawdown, not the standard deviation. The **Calmar ratio** annualises return divided by MaxDD to reward strategies that avoid deep holes.
Exposure is how much of your capital rides on each risk factor; sensitivity is how much value changes per unit of the factor. Three workhorses:

rows: A \$5m book with $\beta = 1.2$ moves like \$6m of market index
Dollar value of one basis point

blocks.md: A hedge is a position with opposite sensitivity of matching size. Beta hedge: to neutralise a \$5m book with $\beta = 1.2$, short \$6m of index futures ($1.2 \times 5m$). Residual risk: the book still carries idiosyncratic risk the index cannot offset, and basis risk, the hedge instrument tracks a slightly different basket than the book.

Duration hedge: the $10m bond position has DV01 $5,000/bp. If a futures contract hedges DV01 \$4,000/bp, the required number of contracts is $5{,}000/4{,}000 = 1.25$, in practice rounded, and imperfect because the future's cheapest-to-deliver bond may drift relative to your bonds. Hedge ratios drift too: as yields and positions move, yesterday's perfect hedge becomes today's residual, which is why desks re-hedge on schedules or thresholds.

blocks.title: Drawdown drives hedging decisions
blocks.md: Many funds cut exposure at a MaxDD trigger (say $-10\%$) to stop the hole deepening, 'de-risking'. This converts drawdown into a control variable: the sensitivity table tells you *what* to reduce, and by how much, to move the portfolio's risk metrics back inside limits.

blocks.title: Hedging removes the risk you measured
blocks.md: A beta hedge eliminates market sensitivity as *measured over the estimation window*. In a regime change, realised beta can differ sharply, the hedge performs worst exactly when you most need it. Treat hedge ratios as estimates under continuous review, never as identities.

guidedExercise.prompt: A fund's monthly values are \$200k, \$230k, \$207k, \$195k, \$240k. Compute the running peaks, each drawdown, the maximum drawdown (in %), and the percentage gain needed from the trough to recover the previous peak.
hints: The peak updates only when value exceeds all prior values.
Recovery gain is measured from the trough to the peak that preceded the drawdown.
guidedExercise.solution: Peaks: $200, 230, 230, 230, 240$. Drawdowns: $0, 0, (207-230)/230 = -10.0\%, (195-230)/230 = -15.2\%, 0$. MaxDD $= 15.2\%$ (230 to 195, a \$35k fall). Recovery needs $35/195 = +17.9\%$ from the trough, bigger than the fall itself, the recovery asymmetry in action.

independentExercise.prompt: A \$20m multi-asset book has $\beta = 0.8$ to the index and holds \$8m of bonds with duration 4. (a) What notional of index futures neutralises the equity beta? (b) What is the book's DV01 from the bond sleeve? (c) If a futures contract has DV01 \$2,500/bp, how many contracts hedge the bond sleeve? (d) Name one risk the hedges do NOT remove.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $0.8 \times 20{,}000{,}000 = \$16m$ short index futures. (b) $8{,}000{,}000 \times 4 \times 0.0001 = $3{,}200$ per bp. (c) $3{,}200/2{,}500 = 1.28$ contracts (round to 1 or 2 in practice, leaving residual). (d) Idiosyncratic risk of the holdings, basis risk between hedges and holdings, and any sensitivity not in the hedge set (e.g. credit spreads).

commonMistakes: Measuring drawdown against the starting value instead of the running peak, the trough must be compared with the highest value before it.
Assuming a 20% loss needs a 20% gain to recover; percentages are asymmetric ($1/(1-0.2) - 1 = 25\%$).
Hedging notional instead of sensitivity: matching dollar amounts is not hedging unless the sensitivities match.
Forgetting that fractional hedge ratios and rounding leave residual exposure that must be monitored.
realWorldApplication: Maximum drawdown appears in every institutional due-diligence questionnaire, drives de-risking triggers and fund terminations, and is the metric most investors remember; DV01 is the daily language of every fixed-income trading desk.
quantFinanceApplication: Risk systems compute running peaks and drawdown series incrementally on every mark, and position systems maintain live sensitivities (beta, DV01, greeks) so the hedging module can compute trade-sized hedge orders automatically.
summary: Drawdown compares each value to the running peak; maximum drawdown is the deepest such gap.
Percentage losses and recovery gains are asymmetric: $-18.6\%$ needs $+22.9\%$ back.
Sensitivities (beta, duration, DV01) convert positions into factor exposures; hedging means offsetting those sensitivities.
Hedges remove the measured sensitivity, leaving basis, idiosyncratic and regime-change risk to monitor.

quiz.prompt: Series: 100, 110, 105, 118, 112, 96 (in \$k). What is the maximum drawdown in %, to one decimal?
After the $-18.6\%$ drawdown to a trough of 96, what percentage gain returns the fund to its 118 peak? To one decimal.
quiz.explanation: $22/96 = 0.2292 \approx +22.9\%$ - larger than the 18.6% fall, the recovery asymmetry.

quiz.prompt: \$10m of bonds, duration 5. DV01 in dollars per basis point?
A book worth \$4m has beta 1.5. The beta-neutralising hedge is:
quiz.explanation: Hedge notional $= \beta \times V = 1.5 \times 4m = \$6m$, with sign opposite to the exposure, short.

quiz.prompt: Which risks survive a beta hedge and a duration hedge executed correctly?
options: Basis risk between hedge instruments and the book
The market sensitivity measured in the estimation window
Model error in the sensitivity estimates themselves
quiz.explanation: Hedges cancel the measured sensitivities only; single-name risk, basis mismatch and estimation error all remain, and (2) is precisely what the hedge removes.

quiz.prompt: Why do investors focus on maximum drawdown rather than volatility when evaluating fund managers?
quiz.modelAnswer: Drawdown captures the worst peak-to-trough loss an investor must endure, it drives redemptions, margin calls and career risk, and is path-dependent in a way symmetric volatility measures are not.
quiz.explanation: Volatility averages fluctuations symmetrically; drawdown records the depth and duration of the worst losing path, which is what investors actually experience and react to.

flashcards.back: $DD_t = (V_t - \max_{s\le t} V_s)/\max_{s\le t} V_s$; maximum drawdown is its most negative value.

flashcards.front: Recovery gain after a drawdown of $d$
flashcards.back: $1/(1+d) - 1$; e.g. a $-20\%$ drawdown needs $+25\%$ to recover.
$DV01 = V \times D \times 0.0001$ - the dollar P&L for a one-basis-point yield move.

flashcards.front: What does a hedge remove: and not remove?
flashcards.back: It cancels the measured sensitivity (beta/duration/DV01); it does not remove basis risk, idiosyncratic risk or errors in the sensitivity estimate.

references.label: Chekhlov, Uryasev & Zabarankin: Drawdown measure in portfolio optimization
